title: Joe Turner Blues
origin: Traditional Tennessee blues about Joe Turney (brother of Governor Pete Turney), who transported prisoners; arranged and published by W. C. Handy, 1915.
note: Public domain: the underlying song is an anonymous nineteenth-century Tennessee blues, and Handy's arrangement was published 1915 (outside the term).
verses:
They tell me Joe Turner's come and gone,
Oh Lordy,
They tell me Joe Turner's come and gone,
Oh Lordy,
Got my man and gone.

He come with forty links of chain,
Oh Lordy,
He come with forty links of chain,
Oh Lordy,
Got my man and gone.

Sweetest man in the whole wide world,
Oh Lordy,
Sweetest man in the whole wide world,
Oh Lordy,
Got my man and gone.

title: Crazy Blues
origin: Perry Bradford (originally titled 'Harlem Blues,' c.1918); recorded by Mamie Smith and published 1920 by Perry Bradford Music Pub. Co.
note: Public domain in the U.S.; published 1920, outside the 95-year term. Landmark as the first vocal blues hit record, recorded by Mamie Smith in 1920.
verses:
I can't sleep at night, I can't eat a bite,
'Cause the man I love, he don't treat me right.
He makes me feel so blue, I don't know what to do.
Sometimes I sit and sigh, and then begin to cry,
'Cause my best man said his last goodbye.

There's a change in the ocean, change in the deep blue sea,
But I'll tell you, folks, there ain't no change in me.
My love for that man will always be.

Now I've got the crazy blues
Since my baby went away,
I ain't got no time to lose,
I must find him today.
